study.title: Musical Sentences
study.question: How do musicians shape phrases?
study.passage:
Phrase shaping (written for this lesson):
1. Find the phrases: most band melodies are in 4-bar phrases. Look for long notes, rests and cadences at the ends. Draw a light pencil arc over each phrase.
2. Find the high point: usually the highest note, a long note, or the note before the cadence. Mark it with an arrow.
3. Shape: grow gently toward the high point, then relax to the cadence, even if the written dynamic stays the same (e.g. mf with a small swell).
4. Speaking test: say a sentence flat, then with expression. Then play a phrase flat, then shaped.
5. Practise with a chorale or a melody like "Ode to Joy" (Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, 1824): 4 bars + 4 bars. Phrase 1 ends open, phrase 2 ends closed.
6. Partner listening: does your partner's phrase "go somewhere"?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Ode to Joy is in the public domain.

study.title: March and Ballad
study.question: How does style change the way we play?
study.passage:
Style guide (written for this lesson):
March: tempo around 112–120 BPM; strong, steady beat (feet could march to it); notes often separated, with accents on strong beats; crisp staccato for accompaniment "oom-pah" parts; clear dynamic contrasts. Form: strains with repeats, often a trio section (usually in a new key, a softer and more lyrical section). Famous example: "The Stars and Stripes Forever" by John Philip Sousa (1896).
Ballad: slow tempo (around 60–76 BPM); legato tonguing and slurs; long phrases with shaping; warm tone; possible rubato led by the conductor.
Activities: 1. Listen to excerpts of each; list features. 2. Play the same 8-bar melody both ways: march style (separated, accented, 116 BPM) and ballad style (legato, shaped, 66 BPM). 3. Apply to the concert pieces: mark style reminders in pencil ("crisp," "smooth," "light").

body.hook: Run out of air in the middle of a phrase and the music breaks apart. Good players plan where to breathe, just like singers and swimmers, so every phrase stays whole.

study.title: Plan Your Breaths
study.question: Where should I breathe in my music?
study.passage:
Breath-planning guide (written for this lesson):
Good places to breathe: at rests; at the end of phrases (look for long notes and cadences); before a new section or a repeat.
Places to avoid: in the middle of a slur; between a tied note; in the middle of a phrase's climb to the high point.
Steps: 1. Sing or hum your part and breathe where it feels natural. 2. Mark breath marks (') in pencil. 3. If there's no rest, time-steal: shorten the note before the breath slightly. 4. Take quick, low breaths through the mouth; practise breathing in for one beat. 5. Long notes beyond your air: use staggered breathing in sections: each player sneaks out, breathes and slides back in quietly at different times, never at bar lines everyone notices.
Practice: mark a breath plan for the concert ballad; play it through; adjust any marks where you still ran out of air. Compare plans with your section so breaths line up in unison passages.
